source.title: Does Moral Reasoning Training Help or Hurt? Red-Teaming RL-Trained Ethical Agents with Persona Attacks

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a difference-in-means activation direction as a steering tool for moral decision-making under persona attacks. It does not test refusal to harmful user requests or refusal of harmless requests, and does not ablate the original refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The reported steering and head-ablation results concern ethical choices under injected personas, not the refusal behavior specified by the claim versions. The paper cites the original refusal-direction study but does not reproduce its refusal measures or intervention. The L21 selection rationale and other values used only to choose settings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the difference-in-means activation-addition technique (it cites Arditi et al.) as a steering tool. The direction is RLMR-Adv minus Base activations on persona-attacked prompts at L21, not harmful minus harmless instructions. The measure is an agentic ethical-choice score under persona attacks, not refusal of harmful requests or induced refusal of harmless ones. No result bears on whether a refusal direction mediates refusal, is removable by weight edit, is suppressed by jailbreaks, is multi-dimensional, transfers, depends on training, or holds in reasoning models.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that structured moral reward, not persona exposure alone, produces persona robustness. They add that a rank-1 L21 direction recovers about 83% of the average gain (about 94% outside Fiction), while Fiction role-play remains a residual linked to competing compliance and alignment heads.
record.recipe_differences: The original defines a harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction and tests removal/addition for refusal. This paper defines an attacked-condition RLMR-Adv-minus-Base direction at L21, adds it at all token positions to steer ethical choices under persona attacks, and also ablates attention heads; it does not test refusal.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effect depends on layer, direction, and injection location: L21 and the cross-model attacked-condition direction work, while tested alternate layers, a within-model direction, and last-token-only injection are reported as null. Steering is attack-dependent, with Fiction much less recoverable. At α≥4000 the model degrades; at α≥8000 it is described as broken.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an RLMR-Adv-minus-Base difference-in-means direction at L21 (α=2000) to Gemma-2-27B Base cuts mean persona-attack degradation from +0.173 to +0.054. Per-attack reductions run from 29% (Fiction) to 72% (Override).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A rank-1 residual-stream direction recovers much of moral-RL persona robustness, with attack-specific limits (Fiction).

fits_no_version.finding: At α=2000 the normal agentic score holds (.063→.059) but ETHICS accuracy drops 3.5pp. The effect is null at other layers, with a within-model direction, and with last-token-only injection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persona-resistance steering is layer-, direction- and position-specific and carries a small accuracy cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Fiction, ablating single heads in RLMR-Adv finds 38 compliance heads and 25 alignment heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persona compliance versus moral alignment involves competing head-level circuits.

fits_no_version.finding: The L21 persona-resistance direction separates attacked from normal inputs in other checkpoints (d=6.22–7.06).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The persona-attack representation is shared across fine-tuned checkpoints of one model.

record.code_released: An anonymized code repository accompanies submission; public release will follow upon acceptance. URL not stated.
record.problems: The paper itself notes that L21 and α=2000 were data-driven choices. The mechanistic analyses are restricted to Gemma-2-27B; head ablations use 30 scenarios. The ETHICS judge is not validated against human moral judgments, and the broader study uses a stylized IPD-to-narrative transfer setting.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded training-condition and general persona-attack robustness tables that do not measure the direction or refusal behavior; excluded layer-wise geometry values used to select L21. The reported results are outside the claim’s refusal construct.

untested.parts: No harmful-minus-harmless direction, no directional ablation, no refusal or compliance rates. Adding the direction targets ethical choices, not refusal.
No weight-edit abliteration of released models.
Persona attacks are measured against moral choices, not against a refusal direction. There is no training against ablation of a refusal direction.
The competing head populations concern Fiction persona compliance in ethical choices, not the geometry of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Cross-checkpoint Cohen's d (r11–r13) concerns a persona-resistance direction, not transfer of a refusal direction.
Moral-reward training conditions are compared for persona robustness, not for whether a refusal direction exists or is removable.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Their states describe the study's own persona-robustness measures, not any claim version. The reported Fiction recovery figure is the 29% reduction versus the Base score (Table 10). Arditi et al. is cited only as precedent for activation engineering.

versions.untested_parts: No refusal direction defined by harmful-minus-harmless instructions; no projection-out ablation across layers and positions; no harmful-request compliance or harmless-request refusal measure.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No test of attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
The competing circuits reported concern persona-resistant ethical choices, not whether refusal is affine, conic, or carried by multiple refusal directions.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Reported direction-transfer measurements concern persona-resistance representations, not transfer of a refusal direction or refusal behavior.
The study compares moral-reward training conditions, but does not test whether refusal training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
